questions.explain: Each step of a dichotomous key splits a group into two.

questions.prompt: Which make GOOD questions for a key? Choose all that apply.
questions.explain: Good questions are about clear, observable features, not opinions or vague sizes.

questions.prompt: In the Key Builder, which question could NOT split the group {butterfly, sparrow}?
questions.explain: Both have wings, so that question doesn't divide them.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest number of yes/no questions a key needs to separate 8 organisms, if every question splits a group exactly in half?
Order the steps for using a key to identify an unknown leaf.
steps: Read the first question in the key
Choose yes or no and follow that branch
Reach the name of the leaf
questions.explain: Keys guide you step by step.

questions.prompt: Design a dichotomous key to identify: a crow, a housefly, a spider, and a cat. Write your questions in order.
questions.modelAnswer: 1) Does it have a backbone? Yes → go to 2. No → go to 3. 2) Does it have feathers? Yes → crow. No → cat. 3) Does it have six legs? Yes → housefly. No (eight legs) → spider.
rubric: Uses yes/no questions on observable features
Each question splits the group into two
Every organism reaches its own name
questions.explain: Criterion B: design a working key.

questions.prompt: Why might ‘Is it brown?’ be a poor question in a key for birds?
options: Colour can vary between males, females, young birds and in different light
Keys can't use colours at all
questions.explain: Choose features that are reliable for every individual.

questions.text: A key helps us ___ an unknown organism by answering ___ questions.
